gnos.title: GNOS Records
gnos.subtitle: Full-Stack · UI/UX Design · Frontend Art
gnos.shortDesc: Designed and developed the complete web visual identity for GNOS Records from scratch. Developer and designer on a living project built to grow alongside the label.
gnos.purposeUsage: Public-facing home of the GNOS Records label — surfaces news, blog, music releases, artists, team and all label information in one editorial space. Live as the label's official web identity for fans, press and industry contacts.
gnos.longDesc: GNOS Records is techno record label with a clear creative identity and the website had to reflect that completely. I created the web visual identity handling everything: UX strategy, visual design, component architecture, and ongoing maintenance. The core design philosophy was emotion first. Every interaction, transition, and layout decision was made with one question in mind: what does the user feel while they're here? The result is a site that doesn't just display information — it creates an atmosphere. Built with React, TypeScript, and Vite, the codebase is architected for scale. As the label grows — more artists, releases, events, editorial content — the system is already designed to absorb that growth without a rebuild. I made every structural decision alone, which means I own the full picture: from the CSS custom properties driving the visual language to the component contracts that keep the UI consistent as new sections are added. This project is ongoing. The current scope covers music and discography, artist profiles, and editorial content. Future phases will introduce new content verticals as the label's catalogue expands.
gnos.aiUsage: AI sat next to me as a co-author across the design and frontend system: rapid component scaffolding from rough sketches, animation-timing exploration through iterative prompts, copy and bilingual translation review, and creative direction sprints. Every output passed through manual taste, refactor and accessibility checks — AI accelerated the creative loop without making the final aesthetic decisions.

highlights.design: Designed, developed, launched and ongoing maintenance
highlights.solo: Solo on the project, no supporting developer
highlights.scale: Built to scale with the label's growth
highlights.ux: UX and emotional experience as primary design driver

juratech.title: LjubenkovicERP
juratech.subtitle: Angular Web Application · ERP Migration
juratech.shortDesc: Led the full frontend migration of a legacy Visual Basic desktop ERP system to a modern Angular web application — sole frontend engineer across a 7-month delivery.
juratech.purposeUsage: ERP for a blinds manufacturer: a Business module where staff configure materials through a Configurator, create work orders and dispatch them to production; and a Workshop module where role-based authorisation profiles serve the right reports and work orders to each operator. Live in daily production at the one manufacturer it was built for — development is ongoing.
juratech.longDesc: LjubenkovicERP is a proprietary ERP platform built for blinds manufacturers, developed at Juratech Solutions. I joined as the sole frontend engineer responsible for translating an entire legacy Visual Basic desktop application into a production-ready Angular web app. The project ran for 7 months. I worked directly alongside the backend and project manager, making architectural decisions on the frontend independently — from component structure and routing to form state management for complex multi-step order workflows. After 3 months, a new backend engineer joined the team. I led his technical onboarding, walked him through the existing API contracts, DTO structure, and frontend integration patterns, and created handover documentation to ensure continuity. The system covers the full operational lifecycle of a manufacturing business: order management, inventory tracking, client records, material and color catalogues, reporting, and user administration — all modules migrated from scratch.
juratech.aiUsage: AI compressed the legacy-to-modern migration loop: TypeScript model drafting from Visual Basic sources, Angular reactive forms patterns, RxJS operator review, unit-test boilerplate, and quick second opinions on edge cases pulled out of the original VB logic. Migration correctness rules and business-critical calculations stayed under manual control — AI's job was speed, not decisions.

unicam.title: Unicam
unicam.subtitle: Product Website · IP Camera & AI Video Analytics
unicam.shortDesc: Designed and developed the public marketing website for Unicam — an AI-powered platform that unifies IP cameras, mobile devices, and video streams into searchable, cloud-backed intelligence.
unicam.purposeUsage: Live at unicam.app as the primary entry point for Unicam's product ecosystem: Platform (AI stream ingestion & LLM video analysis), HUB (cross-platform ONVIF camera management), and native mobile apps. The site targets SMB owners, developers, and enterprise teams — explaining cloud recordings, motion detection, encrypted remote access, webhooks, developer API, and usage-based pricing — and routes visitors to App Store, Google Play, and sales contact.
unicam.longDesc: Unicam is where cameras meet intelligence: a platform that turns real-time footage from IP cameras, old phones, and RTSP/WebRTC/HLS streams into AI-powered insights, alerts, and automation. My work was the public website that has to carry that entire story without drowning the visitor in jargon. The page architecture mirrors the product split — Unicam Platform for LLM-powered video understanding, custom prompts, and business intelligence; Unicam HUB for centralized ONVIF management on macOS, Windows, and Linux; and mobile apps that repurpose devices as live security cameras. Each section translates dense capabilities (object detection, behavioral analysis, cloud recordings, pay-as-you-go AI processing, developer webhooks) into scannable product blocks, testimonial social proof, and FAQ content that still reads clearly for non-technical buyers. Built with React and TypeScript, a component-driven UI on shadcn and Tailwind, fully responsive with store CTAs, and structured for SEO around AI surveillance, ONVIF monitoring, and cloud recording.
unicam.aiUsage: AI accelerated turning raw product specs into clearer marketing structure: drafting section hierarchies for Platform vs HUB vs Mobile, iterating on FAQ and feature copy around protocols like ONVIF, RTSP, and LLM analysis tiers, and exploring layout variants for long technical lists. Every output was manually reviewed for accuracy, tone, and conversion flow — AI sped up the editorial loop without replacing product or brand decisions.

reportify.title: REPORTIFY
reportify.subtitle: Java reporting engine · PostgreSQL → JSON → external API
reportify.shortDesc: Java CLI tool that connects to a PostgreSQL database, generates five different business reports (customer, product, two sales windows, stock) as JSON, and delivers them to an external REST API.
reportify.purposeUsage: Integration layer inside an ERP product: pulls customer, product, sales and stock data from the host database and forwards it on a strict JSON contract to the third-party systems the ERP's clients rely on. Deployed inside the ERP of a previous employer as the connector between their clients and external partner platforms.
reportify.longDesc: Reportify is a Java automation tool that turns operational data sitting in a relational database into structured JSON reports and delivers them straight to an external API. It connects to a PostgreSQL database via JDBC, retrieves customer, product, sales and stock data, transforms each result set into a strictly-defined JSON schema using Gson, and POSTs the resulting payloads to an external REST endpoint using Apache HttpClient. The tool ships as a single JAR with a clean Apache Commons CLI interface — database parameters (host, port, name, user, password) and a comma-separated reports flag are passed at runtime, so the same binary runs against any environment without recompilation. Five report types are supported: customer master data (CUS) with delivery locations, payers, TIN/activity validation rules; product catalogue (PRO) with EAN, measurement units, manufacturer mapping and a multiplier conversion factor; rolling sales (SAL) for the last 14 calendar days with full document/correction tracking (issue date, sale date, correction references, quantity before/after correction); a monthly 35-day sales window sent on the 5th of every month; and stock (STO) — current warehouse status per product and branch. Each report follows a precise field contract — data types, character lengths, mandatory flags and conditional rules (e.g. correction document references being empty for plain sales documents) — so the API consumer can rely on a stable schema. Designed to run unattended via a scheduler, with the report selection chosen per invocation.

highlights.reports: Five report types: customer, product, 14-day & 35-day sales, stock
highlights.database: Direct PostgreSQL access via JDBC — no intermediate layer
highlights.json: Strictly-typed JSON payloads generated with Gson
highlights.api: Delivered to an external REST API via Apache HttpClient POST
highlights.cli: Single JAR with CLI flags — environment-agnostic deployments

cer.title: CER
cer.subtitle: Currency Exchange Rate · Java algorithm + NBS integration
cer.shortDesc: Java algorithm that fetches the official daily exchange rate list from the National Bank of Serbia, parses the SOAP response, and stores each currency into PostgreSQL — scheduled to run automatically every working morning.
cer.purposeUsage: Feeds the ERP's currency module with the official NBS rates each user has flagged, so they never have to open the NBS website to check a rate themselves. Deployed inside the ERP of a previous employer — the algorithm guarantees that the rates shown to users match the official NBS publication for the current day.
cer.longDesc: CER (Currency Exchange Rate) is my first more complex algorithm — a Java 17 application that runs on a daily schedule and connects to the National Bank of Serbia's SOAP web service to retrieve the official exchange rate list published every working morning at 8 AM. The program parses the XML response with Jakarta XML Bind, validates the data and persists every currency record into a PostgreSQL database. All database parameters (host, port, name, user, password) are passed at runtime through the command line via Apache Commons CLI, which makes the tool environment-agnostic — the same JAR runs against any database instance without a rebuild. Authentication against the NBS service is handled through the Metro Glassfish Web Services Runtime, using credentials and a license issued directly by NBS and sent over Apache HttpClient. A CRON / time-scheduler task triggers the JAR every working morning after 8 AM with the appropriate connection parameters, so the data is always up to date by the start of the business day. CER is integrated into Melany Software ERP as the engine behind the Exchange Rates interface — users can view the latest rates and add new currencies to the daily fetch loop, with the algorithm handling the rest automatically.

highlights.algorithm: First more complex algorithm — fully automated end-to-end
highlights.nbs: Integrated with the National Bank of Serbia SOAP service
highlights.scheduler: Runs daily after 8 AM via CRON scheduled task
highlights.erp: Powers the Exchange Rates module inside Melany Software ERP

rotation1Modal.pick: Twelve spokes, one property — rotate() is the whole trick here.

rotation2Modal.pick: Nine pivots, one rotation — the outline stays, the fill shows where 45° lands.

rotation3Modal.pick: The wireframe stays flat; the plate leans on a diagonal axis in space.

rotation4Modal.pick: rotate() in a loop — static ring, one beam doing the timekeeping.

overlap1Modal.pro1: One loop, one number to change — suddenly you have 3, 6, or 12 petals instead of 6. CSS does not care how many circles exist, and it does not need to.
overlap1Modal.con1: rotate and translate are married — order matters. Swap the order and the circle flies the wrong way until you sit down and sketch it on paper.
overlap1Modal.pick: Whenever the element count is not fixed — icons in a ring, animated loading rings, anything where the client can say "add one more."

overlap2Modal.pro1: Open DevTools and you immediately see what is where. No matrix, no trig — just top: 40px, left: 60px, done.
overlap2Modal.con1: Every new circle means new coordinates you calculate or measure by hand. For 6 circles — fine. For 24 — no thanks.
overlap2Modal.pick: When the designer hands you a Figma file with exact positions and that layout will never change. Marketing heroes, poster elements, decorative details.

overlap3Modal.pro1: Every element sits in the same grid cell and overlaps naturally, without any element "knowing" about the others. Clean and readable in code.
overlap3Modal.con1: Grid gives you the stack, not the layout — you still need transform to position. Two systems together can confuse you if you are not clear which part does what.
overlap3Modal.pick: Badge on an avatar, multiple icons in one slot, notification indicators — when you layer elements without a radial layout.

overlap4Modal.pro1: Angle and distance live on two separate elements — the parent sets direction, the child sets how far. Logic stays clear and scales to 24, 48, as many circles as you need.
overlap4Modal.con1: Two DOM nodes per circle instead of one. Not a performance issue, but the HTML is twice as long as it needs to be.
overlap4Modal.pick: Dense rings, mandalas, a clock with dots on the rim — any pattern with many elements at the same distance from the center.
